title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E526 studies transverse vibrations of elastic rods (laminae/virgae). Notation: arc length s, abscissa x (equal to s for small deflections), deflection y(s,t), cross-section proportional to cc (so mass per unit length is proportional to cc), flexural rigidity bc^4 (proportional to the fourth power of the thickness, as for second moment of area times modulus). The factor 1/2g comes from Euler's time units, in which acceleration is measured against gravity. The previous page derived the mixed equation (1/2g) y_tt = h y_ss - bcc y_ssss for a rod also under axial tension cch, i.e. the stiff string. 

On this page (Scholion, §8), Euler makes three modelling choices:
- He drops all axial (tensile or compressive) forces from the rest of the memoir, because they complicate the final equation.
- He allows only forces F acting normally to the rod.
- He assumes the rod is naturally straight, of uniform thickness and uniform elasticity.

Because the final equation was obtained by differentiating twice, he lists the hierarchy of integrated equations:
- I (moment balance): -F x + (cc/2g) ∫dx ∫ds y_tt = -bc^4 y_ss. The bending moment bc^4·curvature equals the moment of the inertial forces and of the transverse force F.
- II (shear balance): -F + (cc/2g) ∫ds y_tt = -bc^4 y_sss.
- III, the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation: (cc/2g) y_tt = -bc^4 y_ssss, or (1/2g) y_tt = -bcc y_ssss.

F enters only I and II. It must be retained when the rod is pinned at one or more points by a 'stylus' (a pivot about which the rod can still rotate). Such a point support contributes a concentrated transverse reaction, i.e. a jump in the shear force, while the bending moment stays continuous. Euler notes that the rod can be fixed by such styli in infinitely many ways, each modifying the motion. These cases (supported, free, clamped ends, and intermediate supports) are to be treated next, beginning with separation of variables y = M(s) sin(ζ + t√(2g/k)) on the following page.
errors: No mathematical errors. Differentiating I with x≈s gives II, and differentiating II gives III, with consistent signs. Dividing III by cc gives the second form correctly. The identification dx≈ds is the usual small-deflection approximation and is left implicit.

ideas.what: Hierarchy of moment, shear and fourth-order equations for a vibrating beam, with transverse point forces at supports entering only the lower-order (integrated) forms
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli beam equation with moment/shear relations; point-support reactions as shear jumps
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Daniel Bernoulli (1734–1744), refined by Euler in the 1770s papers on vibrating rods
ideas.where_published: E526 itself; also earlier treatments in Euler's 1744 Methodus inveniendi (Additamentum I) and the 1770s papers on rod vibration; discussed by Truesdell, Opera omnia II.11/2

ideas.what: Deliberate exclusion of axial tension/compression (the stiff-string equation of the previous page) from the remainder of the study
ideas.modern_name: Stiff string / beam under axial load equation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (this memoir); stiff-string equation later studied by Seebeck, Rayleigh and others

ideas.what: Intermediate pin supports ('styli') allowing rotation but not displacement, giving infinitely many support configurations
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E526); later systematic multi-span beam theory (Clapeyron three-moment equation, 1857)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a transitional scholion that restates well-known beam equations and sets up the boundary-condition study. Euler's work on vibrating rods is thoroughly documented by Truesdell.
transcription_corrections: The 'aquationes' in the transcription is a misprint present in the original print (for 'aequationes'), not an OCR error.
Page header '111' is the printed page number; the transcription matches the image otherwise.
